## 1. Why this phase, and why now

Three things earned their way into this phase, all called out explicitly in Memory.md rather than invented for this prompt:

1. **IPD billing does not exist.** A Tier 2 clinic can admit a patient to a bed (`admit_patient_to_bed()`, Phase 3) and the encounter becomes an inpatient stay — but nothing charges for it. `billing_line_items.source_type` has `consultation`, `medicine`, `lab`, `procedure`, `other`. There is no `room_rent`/`bed_day` category, no rate, no mechanism. For a clinic actually running a ward, this isn't a missing nice-to-have — it's the thing that makes Tier 2 a real product rather than a bed-tracking demo.
2. **`admit_patient_to_bed()` locks the two beds in a transfer target-then-source, not canonically** — diagnosed in Phase 5, deliberately not fixed there because that phase's remit was the *reported* race, not every latent one found while auditing it. It's still sitting there with a stated fix nobody's applied.
3. **Cancelling an issued prescription has no RPC**, despite `cancelled` existing in the status enum and `record_medication_administration()` already checking for it and returning `PRESCRIPTION_CANCELLED`. The guard has been ready and waiting since Phase 3.

Item 1 is the centerpiece and is genuinely a full phase's worth of design work. Items 2 and 3 are small, fully diagnosed already, and touch the same tables — bundle them in rather than spinning up a separate prompt for two paragraphs of fix.

**Deliberately not in this phase**, and don't let scope creep pull them in: multi-branch/tenant hierarchy (needs a product decision about what a "branch" even is — not a schema problem), blood-bank cross-matching (a clinical lab procedure, not something a database constraint can provide safety for), audit-log retention and read-auditing (Memory.md's own words: "needs a policy decision, not code, first"), the insurance/TPA submission-format generator (Tier 3, no pilot clinic needs it yet), patient portal / "my own record" access (a real future phase, but a distinct concern from billing — don't merge two unrelated new surfaces into one migration set).

## 2. IPD Billing — the centerpiece

### 2.1 The GST rule you're building against — verified, not assumed

I looked this up rather than guessing, because Phase 2 already set the standard for getting healthcare GST right and this deserves the same rigor. Since 18 July 2022 (GST Council, and reaffirmed since), hospital room charges follow a **third** category distinct from the consultation/medicine split already in `resolve_tax_treatment()`:

- **ICU, CCU, intensive cardiac care, and NICU rooms are fully GST-exempt, regardless of the rate charged.**
- **Every other room is exempt if the rate is ≤ ₹5,000/day, and taxable at a flat 5% (with no input tax credit available to the hospital) the moment the rate exceeds ₹5,000/day.**

Sources: [ClearTax](https://cleartax.in/s/gst-on-hospital-room-rent-beds), [SBI General](https://www.sbigeneral.in/blog/health-insurance/health-articles/gst-on-hospital-room-rent), [Grant Thornton](https://www.grantthornton.in/insights/blogs/gst-on-hospital-room-rent-a-bitter-pill-to-swallow/), consistent across all three. Content paraphrased for compliance with reproduction limits.

**Consequence for the schema:** taxability depends on two things that don't exist yet — a per-bed/per-ward **critical-care flag** and a **daily rate**. Both need adding. Follow the pattern already established for `default_consultation_fee` and GSTIN: **snapshot the rate onto the billing line at the moment it's charged**, not looked up live from `beds` at invoice time — a ward's rate changing next month must not retroactively change what a bed-day charged three weeks ago.

### 2.2 Schema — your call on exact shape, principles below are not optional

- Add a critical-care flag and a daily rate to `beds` (or to a new lightweight ward-classification concept, if you judge the free-text `ward_name` has outgrown itself — but re-read the Phase 3 comment that explicitly rejected a `wards` table "for now," and that "now" was specifically deferred until ward-level attributes like a per-day rate were needed. **That moment is this phase.** Decide and document whether this is the trigger for that table finally existing, or whether a rate/flag directly on `beds` is still sufficient — either is defensible, but say which and why).
- Extend `billing_line_items.source_type`'s CHECK constraint to add a room-rent category (name it what you think reads best — `room_rent` or `bed_day`, pick one, be consistent). New migration, obviously — the existing constraint is applied and stays as history.
- Extend `resolve_tax_treatment()` (don't duplicate its logic — it already correctly handles consultation-exempt and medicine-taxable-with-exceptions; add the third case to the same function) with the ICU-exempt / ≤₹5000-exempt / >₹5000-taxable-5%-no-ITC branching from §2.1.

### 2.3 The scheduled-job problem — this is the real design question, and it's yours to resolve, not mine to dictate

Nothing in this stack runs on a schedule. Every trigger fires on an event (an insert, a status change); nothing fires "at midnight" or "every N hours." Bed-day billing is inherently periodic — a charge for each night of a stay — so this phase is the first time that gap actually matters.

Investigate, and document what you actually find rather than assuming:

- **Is the `pg_cron` extension available on this hosted project's plan?** If yes, and you can verify it (the same way Phase 5 verified WAL archiving directly rather than assuming), a nightly job posting a bed-day charge for every currently-occupied bed is the closest fit to "bill for each night as it happens."
- **Supabase's own platform-level Cron** (scheduled Edge Function triggers) needs a deployed Edge Function, which needs a personal access token this machine doesn't have — same blocker as the three Edge Functions already sitting undeployed since Phase 2/3.
- **An on-demand alternative that needs no scheduler at all**: compute the full bed-day charge in one shot — walking `admitted_at` through `discharged_at` (or through "now" for an ongoing stay) in nightly segments — at the moment an invoice is actually raised, rather than posting one line per night as each night passes. This trades "billing staff can see the running total accruing day by day" for "nothing needs infrastructure this project has never used and can't currently verify."

**Do not build a scheduler you can't test.** If `pg_cron` isn't confirmably available and working here the same way WAL archiving was confirmably verified in Phase 5, don't ship code that depends on it running — that's exactly the "fake infra you can't verify" mistake this project has consistently avoided (see: not building a stub `apps/web` for Playwright, not writing an automated backup job against an unknown plan tier). Pick the approach you can actually prove works, say which one and why, and log the other as a documented future item once either `pg_cron` is confirmed or a PAT unblocks Edge Function deployment.

### 2.4 The idempotency question — look at precedent before designing this from scratch

Every existing auto-billing trigger in this schema solved "how do we charge exactly once" a different way, and each solution matches its own event shape:
- Consultation charging fires on a `visits.status` transition and is idempotent by re-entering the same status not double-charging.
- Medicine charging fires on prescription `issue`, a one-shot lifecycle transition.
- Lab charging fires on order insert, a single event with a single charge.

Bed-day billing doesn't have a single natural "this happened once" event the way those do — a stay accrues continuously. Decide what the billable event actually is under whichever mechanism you chose in §2.3 (a nightly cron tick? invoice-time computation covering the whole stay-so-far?), and design the idempotency/uniqueness guarantee around that specific shape — don't force-fit the consultation or medicine pattern if it doesn't match. The existing `billing_one_line_per_source_idx` (`unique (tenant_id, source_type, source_id) where source_id is not null`) may or may not apply depending on what you decide `source_id` should even point to for a bed-day charge (the bed? the visit? a new concept representing "this stay" or "this night"?) — this is a real modeling decision, work it through rather than picking the first thing that compiles.

### 2.5 Discharge and mid-stay changes

- What happens to accrued-but-uncharged bed-days at discharge? A stay that ends mid-cycle (whatever cycle your §2.3 design uses) needs its final partial charge captured, not silently dropped.
- What happens if a patient transfers between wards with different rates mid-stay (the transfer path already exists in `admit_patient_to_bed()`)? The rate applicable to each night should reflect whichever ward they were actually in that night — this is exactly why the rate must be snapshotted per charge, not looked up once for the whole stay.

## 3. Two small, already-diagnosed fixes — bundle these in, don't skip them

### 3.1 `admit_patient_to_bed()` bed-lock ordering (Phase 5 finding, not yet fixed)

Transfers currently lock the two beds target-then-source. Two simultaneous mirror-image transfers (clinic A moves a patient bed1→bed2 while, coincidentally, bed2→bed1 is also in flight) can deadlock on `beds` alone. Fix: lock the two bed rows in a deterministic order (e.g., by `id`) regardless of which is "target" and which is "source." Low real-world likelihood, non-silent when it happens (`40P01`, one side cleanly aborts and can retry) — but it's a real bug with a stated fix sitting unapplied. New migration; the existing function isn't broken enough to justify skipping this, just imprecise.

### 3.2 `cancel_prescription()` — the guard has been waiting since Phase 3

Add the RPC. `record_medication_administration()` already returns `PRESCRIPTION_CANCELLED` for a cancelled prescription, so the read side is done — only the write path (the transition itself) is missing. Follow the `draft → issued` lifecycle's existing pattern: what can be cancelled (a `draft` trivially; an `issued` prescription probably needs a reason, since medicine charges may have already been auto-captured — decide whether cancelling after issue reverses/voids those billing lines or leaves them and relies on the reconciliation view to surface the discrepancy, and document which). Add the contract update to `docs/contracts/prescriptions.md`.

## 5. Boundaries (unchanged, repeated because they still apply)

1. Never bypass RLS; no service-role key outside a local dev script or a stated, narrow exception with a documented reason.
2. Never trust a client-passed `tenant_id`.
3. Never log patient PII/PHI.
4. No new backend server, ORM, or hosting provider — and no scheduled-job mechanism you haven't verified actually runs on this project (see §2.3).
5. Migrations are additive history — new file, never edit an applied one.
6. Do not touch `apps/web`, and do not create anything under it.
7. Tier gating: bed-day billing is a Tier 2+ concern by definition (no beds exist below Tier 2), but confirm this falls out naturally from the existing bed/admission gating rather than needing a second, separate check — don't gate the same thing twice in two different places.
